paper_title: Training Vision Transformers to Focus: Emergence of Spatial Attention Head Specialization

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Self-supervised learning in Vision Transformer models, such as DINO, enables robust visual perception without requiring labeled data by leveraging large-scale image datasets. However, these models lack a focusing mechanism during training, resulting in perceptual representations that are often ambiguous or overly similar. In this work, we introduce two visual focusing loss functions designed to establish correspondence between the model's attention and specific regions within images. Specifically, we leverage the multi-head attention mechanism within the model to selectively steer the model's focus, leading to the emergence of spatial attention head specialization, characterized by diverse and spatially focused perceptual capabilities without requiring annotations. Through both qualitative and quantitative evaluations, we demonstrate that our method substantially increases the spatial selectivity and diversity of attention heads, improving both interpretability and performance on dense prediction tasks such as zero-shot image segmentation.

Existing learned perceptual representations (left) in individual attention heads often tend to be ambiguous or overly similar within the example image and across images in the dataset, which limits their interpretability. sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Self-supervised learning has become powerful paradigm in computer vision, enabling models to acquire rich and meaningful visual representations without the need for costly and time-consuming 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). labeled data. Among various architectures, Vision Transformers (ViTs) (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) have attracted considerable attention for their remarkable ability to capture long-range dependencies and complex visual patterns within images. Methods such as Self-Distillation with No Labels (DINO) (Caron et al., 2021) have demonstrated that large-scale unlabeled image datasets can effectively train ViTs to produce robust and transferable visual features. Despite these advances, fundamental challenge remains: unlike supervised approaches that rely on explicit guidance via labels or self-supervised approaches that incorporate prior knowledge to guide attention, self-supervised ViT models without such explicit guidance or prior knowledge typically lack focusing mechanism during training. Consequently, the learned perceptual representations often tend to be ambiguous or overly similar across attention heads, which limits their discriminative capacity and interpretability. Addressing this limitation is crucial for extending the applicability of self-supervised ViTs, particularly in tasks that require dense representations such as object segmentation and interpretability analysis. To this end, we propose two visual focusing loss functions that establish correspondence between the models attention and specific regions within images during training. We refer to this correspondence as region-to-focus correspondence (ReFoCo). The first loss, the inside-focus loss, is designed to align the models focus on local regions within images with the cropped images of these corresponding regions. The second loss is inspired by weakly-supervised learning with masked images as proposed in Kumar Singh and Jae Lee (2017), where masking forces the model to focus not only on the most discriminative object parts, but also on other regions. Our proposed second loss, the outside-focus loss, is designed to achieve similar effect in self-supervised manner by associating partially masked images with the models focus on regions outside the masked parts. Our approach leverages the multi-head attention mechanism in ViTs to selectively steer the models focus, and we find that diverse and spatially focused perceptual capabilities emerge in our trained model, as shown in Fig. 1. Our method also substantially improves the models interpretability. We conduct extensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations to validate the effectiveness of our approach. The results demonstrate that incorporating our visual focusing losses substantially improves the models ability to localize and differentiate between various image regions. These improvements lead to higher zero-shot image segmentation performance, unsupervised object discovery performance, and multi-object image retrieval performance, along with clearer and more interpretable attention maps, highlighting the practical advantages of our method. We note that while the proposed losses encourage the emergence of diverse and spatially focused perceptual capabilities, we observe slight reduction in classification performance. Accordingly, our results should not be interpreted as demonstrating universally stronger global or dense representations. Rather, our method aims to introduce focusing mechanisms into self-supervised ViT learning without requiring annotations, encouraging attention heads to capture diverse and spatially focused visual information. Overall, our contributions are as follows: We identify the ambiguity and similarity of perceptual representations present in current self-supervised ViT models, which limits their interpretability. We present new direction for introducing focusing mechanisms into self-supervised ViTs learning without requiring annotations, using visual focusing loss functions that link representation learning more directly to visual understanding. We evaluate the performance of models trained using our visual focusing loss functions and demonstrate that they achieve higher zero-shot image segmentation performance, unsupervised object discovery performance, and multi-object image retrieval performance, while also producing more interpretable and meaningful attention maps.

sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Vision Transformers and self-supervised learning. The advent of ViTs (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) has ushered in paradigm shift in self-supervised learning. Leveraging their global receptive fields and adaptive attention mechanisms, ViTs effectively capture long-range dependencies that conventional convolutional neural networks (Simonyan and Zisserman, 2015; He et al., 2016) typically struggle to model. Techniques such as DINO (Caron et al., 2021) and iBOT (Zhou et al., 2022) have demonstrated that ViTs are effective at learning structured, semantically rich representations without the need for 2 labeled data. Remarkably, both DINO and its successor, DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024), shows that ViTs can generate attention maps closely aligned with object boundaries, suggesting an emergent capacity for dense visual recognition. Visual focusing mechanisms. However, existing self-supervised ViT methods often lack effective focusing mechanisms during training. Consequently, multiple attention heads tend to converge toward similar activation patterns, producing ambiguous or redundant representations (Bhojanapalli et al., 2021). Some approaches have attempted to mitigate this issue by promoting attention map diversification (Ren et al., 2025), employing block dropping (Bhojanapalli et al., 2021), or knowledge distillation (Wu et al., 2022) techniques to reduce redundancy. However, these strategies are typically indirect, relying on architectural heuristics rather than explicitly designed loss functions that encourage interpretability or spatial differentiation. Post-hoc explanation methods, such as attention rollout (Abnar and Zuidema, 2020; Jo et al., 2025) and gradient-based techniques (Selvaraju et al., 2017), can reveal where the model focuses after training but do not influence the training dynamics. Other efforts have introduced architectural modifications (Chen et al., 2023), add-on modules (Lee et al., 2021), or prior knowledge-guidance (Miao et al., 2022) to foster diversity across attention heads or enhance spatial localization. Yet these methods often require supervision or additional annotations, limiting their applicability in fully self-supervised settings. In summary, although current methods successfully capture global structure and high-level semantics, they often lack mechanisms that promote diverse, meaningful, and discriminative attention across different image regions. The proposed visual focusing losses offer principled approach to encourage spatial specialization, enhancing interpretability within self-supervised ViT frameworks. Integrating such focusing mechanisms that shape attention during training is relatively unexplored direction with the potential to link self-supervised representation learning to transparent and spatially grounded visual reasoning. Visual prompt techniques. Inspired by prompt engineering in natural language processing (Brown et al., 2020), variety of visual prompts have been studied in computer vision to intuitively modify the behavior of models in visual manner (Kirillov et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023; Shtedritski et al., 2023; Zhuang et al., 2024; Jia et al., 2022; Park and Byun, 2024; Yoo et al., 2023; Bahng et al., 2022; Nozawa et al., 2025). In this work, to selectively steer the models focus, we leverage visual prompting technique called prompt-guided attention head selection (PHS) (Nozawa et al., 2025). In PHS, the visual prompt is given as set of binary values assigned to each pixel in the image, where each value indicates whether it is included in the region of interest (ROI) or not. This has the advantage that the shape of the ROI is not restricted.

sections.title: 3 Proposed method
sections.content: We consider self-supervised learning settings, such as DINO (Caron et al., 2021), where teacher and student models are used and training is performed by minimizing loss function between the two models. To enable the model to acquire the ability to focus on the ROI, we propose to introduce two visual focusing loss functions as shown in Fig. 2. First, we briefly introduce the PHS method (Nozawa et al., 2025) for modifying the models output using the ROI. Once the ROI is specified, the attention heads that produce the largest outputs of attention maps within the ROI are selected. By applying the head selection method (Gong et al., 2021; Meng et al., 2022; Ni et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2022; Nicolicioiu et al., 2023; Basile et al., 2025) that emphasizes the outputs of the selected heads, the models overall output is modified to align with the ROI. Formally, let = {1, 2, . . . , h} denote the set of the heads, and let ion be the set of the selected heads. The Multi-Head Attention in the last attention layer, Linear ([head1, head2, . . . , headh]) is then modified by replacing headi with headHS , defined by headHS = (cid:26)headi h/hon 0 if ion, if / ion, (1) where hon = ion is the number of the selected heads. As result, for each input image x, the models output (x) changes to PHS(x, R). Figure 2: Overview of our proposed visual focusing loss functions Lin and Lout. Inside-focus loss. The first loss function aims to align the models focus on local areas within images with the cropped images of these corresponding areas. For each training image x, we designate box bx within the image as the ROI. Then, the cropped image corresponding to the box, denoted as xcrop, is input to the teacher model. Meanwhile, the entire image is input to the student model. However, instead of simply providing the input to the student model, we apply the PHS (Nozawa et al., 2025) method, which enhances the intermediate outputs related to the ROI within the model as described above. The inside-focus loss function Lin is defined as the cross-entropy loss between the outputs of the teacher and student networks: Lin = 1 (cid:88) Pt(xcrop) log PHS (x, = bx), (2) where is the batch size, the summation runs over the batch, Pt denotes the softmax output of the teacher network, and PHS represents the softmax output of the student network with PHS visually prompting the box bx applied. Outside-focus loss. To enable the model to focus not only on the most discriminative object or part but also on other regions, we introduce another loss function. Similar to the inside-focus loss function Lin, we designate box bx as the ROI for each image x. However, for the teacher model in this case, we input the image in which the region within the box is masked, denoted as xmask. For the student model, the entire image is input, similar to the case of Lin. The difference is the use of PHS, which utilizes the external region of the box, bx, as visual prompt. The outside-focus loss function Lout is then given by the following cross-entropy loss: Lout = 1 (cid:88) Pt(xmask) log PHS (x, = bx). (3) We propose that by combining these visual focusing loss functions with conventional loss functions used in self-supervised learning, the model effectively acquire the ability to focus on various objects or regions within the images.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: 4.1 Interpretability comparison of attention maps for conventional training methods Since our training method utilizes attention maps via PHS, interpretability of the maps is crucial. To determine the training method adopted in our method, we compare the attention maps of four different 4 Figure 3: Comparison of the average of attention maps on ImageNet-1k across four training methods using pretrained models (a)-(d). training methods: DeiT III (Touvron et al., 2022), CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024) and DINOv2 with registers (Darcet et al., 2024), utilizing publicly available pretrained models. DeiT III is label-supervised training method for ViTs. CLIP is text-supervised training method using contrastive learning on image-text pairs. DINOv2 with and without registers are self-supervised training methods to learn robust visual representations. DINOv2 with registers extends DINOv2 by introducing additional register tokens to get rid of high-norm tokens in attention maps, which is called artifacts (Darcet et al., 2024). More details about the pretrained models are described in Sec. C.1. Figure 3 shows the average of the attention maps and the head mean of them on the validation set of ImageNet-1k (Russakovsky et al., 2015). Artifacts are observed in the maps produced by DeiT III, CLIP, and DINOv2, which is consistent with Darcet et al. (2024), whereas the maps generated by DINOv2 with registers are clearer. Based on this result and extended analysis presented in Sec. D.1, we adopt DINOv2 with registers as the baseline training method. 4.2 Training We train ViT models with registers (Darcet et al., 2024) using DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024) as the baseline training method to study the effects of incorporating our proposed loss functions on the models performance. We mainly follow the learning process of DINOv2, but we replace the original DINOv2 loss LDINOv2 = LDINO + LiBOT + 0.1 Lkoleo with the following loss function: Lfocus = (1 win wout) LDINO + win Lin + wout Lout + LiBOT + 0.1 Lkoleo, (4) where win and wout are the weights of the visual focusing loss functions Lin and Lout in Eqs. (2) and (3), respectively. We note that the DINO loss LDINO is cross-entropy loss of the same type as Lin and Lout; therefore, its magnitude is comparable to that of Lin and Lout. LiBOT is the iBOT loss (Zhou et al., 2022), Lkoleo is the KoLeo loss (Sablayrolles et al., 2019), and for win = 0 and wout = 0, Eq. (4) reduces to the DINOv2 loss. For each training image x, we designate one box bx, which is specified as random local region within the image, analogous to the local crops used in DINO (Caron et al., 2021). We share the box bx for the computation of both Lin and Lout. Notably, because the boxes can be designated randomly during training, our approach requires only the images as training data and does not necessitate any ground truth data, such as the positional information of objects within the images. We train the ViT models on the train split of ImageNet-1k dataset (Russakovsky et al., 2015) without labels and use the teacher model in all evaluation experiments. Except for the continual learning discussed in Sec. D.2, the models are trained from scratch. Unless otherwise stated, we use ViT-L/16 with registers (ViT-L/16Reg) (Darcet et al., 2024) and compare models trained under four different loss weight settings: (1) DINOv2 (win = 0, wout = 0), (2) DINOv2 with Lin (win = 0.1, wout = 0), (3) DINOv2 with Lout (win = 0, wout = 0.1), and (4) DINOv2 with Lin and Lout (win = 0.05, wout = 0.05). More details about the training conditions are described in Sec. C.1. 5 Table 1: Zero-shot image segmentation performance. The DINOv2 model that integrates both Lin and Lout outperforms the original DINOv2 model on both ImageNet-Segmentation and PASCAL VOC. (Model: ViT-L/16-Reg) ImageNet-Seg. We follow standard protocol (Chefer et al., 2021) for evaluating the effectiveness of their heat maps. For each heat map, we compute the head mean of the attention maps, where we use the [CLS] tokens from each head in the last attention layer as the attention maps. We then binarize the heat map into foreground/background segmentation map, where the patch mean of the heat map is used for the threshold value. We utilize two datasets, ImageNet-Segmentation (Guillaumin et al., 2014) and PASCAL VOC (Everingham et al., 2010), for the evaluation following Chefer et al. (2021) and Helbling et al. (2025). ImageNet-Segmentation consists of 4,276 single-label images from the validation set of ImageNet-1k (Russakovsky et al., 2015) with annotated segmentations from 445 categories. For the evaluation on PASCAL VOC, we utilize PASCAL VOC 2012 benchmark (Everingham et al., 2015) and evaluate on multi-class split (1,449 images). In our multi-class split experiment, all annotated objects are considered as single foreground. Quantitative evaluation results. To investigate the impact of changes to the loss function, we quantitatively evaluate zero-shot image segmentation performance using three standard evaluation metrics: mean Intersection over Union (mIoU), pixel-wise accuracy (Acc), and mean Average Precision (mAP). Table 1 provides comparison of zero-shot image segmentation performance for models trained using four different loss functions. The results indicate that the performance of the DINOv2 models with either Lin alone or Lout alone is comparable to that of the original DINOv2 model. In contrast, the model with both Lin and Lout outperforms all the other models across all the evaluation metrics. 4.4 Qualitative analysis and emergent abilities Dataset-scale attention heads visualization. To investigate which regions of the images the models focus on, we visualize the average of the attention maps across the entire set of evaluation dataset images. Figure 4 shows the average of the attention maps and the head mean of them used as the heat map on the validation set of ImageNet-1k. As result, we find that the visual loss functions qualitatively change the characteristics of attention maps. Emergent focusing ability: Spatial Attention Head Specialization. As shown in Fig. 4(a), the attention maps of each head in the original DINOv2 model mainly concentrate their outputs around the center. In contrast, as illustrated in Fig. 4(b), the model with Lin shows substantial variety in the output locations across different heads. This visualizes the emergence of the ability for each head to focus on distinct spatial positions, and their information is integrated to produce the comprehensive heat map. Notably, the focus area of the heat map in this model is broader compared to that of the original model. In the model with Lout, in addition to heads that primarily focus on the central region as seen in the original model, there also emerge heads that tend to avoid the center and focus on other regions. This behavior is considered to reflect the design of Lout, which encourages attention to objects other than the most discriminative objects. Additionally, large activation is observed in single patch at the top-left corner, which is considered to be type of artifact, as discussed in Darcet et al. (2024). As described above, by using Lin and Lout, various attention behaviors emerge across different heads. In the model with both Lin and Lout, we observe the coexistence of the attention 6 Figure 4: Comparison of the average of attention maps on ImageNet-1k from head1 to head16 and their head mean. Each model is trained using one of four loss functions (a)-(d). Figure 5: An example of attention maps for each model (a)-(d). The image in the top left is the input. The images labeled mean represent the head means of the attention maps used as heat maps, and the images labeled mask represent the segmentation masks. maps observed in the model with Lin alone or Lout alone, in addition to attention maps that focus on broader regions. We note that the artifacts seen in the model with Lout alone are absent. While standard DINOv2 already exhibits content-based head specialization, with individual heads capturing different semantic features within an image, our method retains such content-based specialization while introducing an additional, complementary form of specialization across spatial regions. We refer to this phenomenon as the emergence of spatial attention head specialization. 4.5 Empirical analysis of segmentation capability To understand how segmentation works on individual images, we analyze examples of attention maps for specific input image, as shown in Fig. 5. In the case of the original DINOv2 model, we observe that all heads focus at least partially on the box behind the donuts, which leads to ambiguous segmentation. We speculate that the original model pays close attention to the box because part of the box is visible in the center of the input image. When Lin is introduced, we observe that the model focus on object regions corresponding to the parts discussed in the attention map averages in Fig. 4. For instance, head1, 7, 11, and 15 in Fig. 5(d) are able to focus primarily on each donut region in the image. Furthermore, when Lout is introduced, as seen in head8 of Fig. 5(d), there emerge attention heads that focus on the box regions while avoiding the donuts area. This corresponds to the heads focusing on non-central regions on average, as discussed in Sec. 4.4. 4.6 Segmentation performance by position As shown in Tab. 1, we find that the model with Lin and Lout exhibits higher segmentation performance compared to the other models evaluated. To investigate the positional dependence of 7 Figure 6: Changes in segmentation accuracy at each position compared to the accuracy of the original DINOv2 model. Table 2: Unsupervised object discovery performance. (Model: ViT-L/16-Reg) Table 3: ImageNet-1k classification performance. (Model: ViT-L/16-Reg) Loss VOC07 VOC12 COCO Loss k-NN (%) Linear (%) DINOv2 w/ Lin w/ Lout w/ Lin & Lout 58.6 56.0 42.0 61.6 63.3 59.5 47.3 64.6 45.4 45.7 35.1 45.5 DINOv2 w/ Lin w/ Lout w/ Lin & Lout 81.7 79.1 79.7 80.3 82.6 81.4 81.7 81. performance among the models, we calculate the accuracy at each position for each model and examine the changes in accuracy from the original model, referred to as Accpos as shown in Fig. 6. The figure shows that Lin and Lout play complementary roles in improving segmentation accuracy. First, as shown in Fig. 6(a), the model with Lin alone decreases accuracy in the central region while improving accuracy in the peripheral regions. This result suggests that whereas the original DINOv2 model tends to focus on objects near the center, Lin encourages attention to various regions, which enhances segmentation performance in less salient peripheral areas while somewhat reducing focus on the center. In contrast, Fig. 6(b) shows that the model with Lout alone exhibits improved accuracy in ring-shaped region surrounding the center. This result can be interpreted as indicating that Lout primarily enhances segmentation performance in regions surrounding central objects, which are typically located in the center. Although each of these two models shows improved segmentation performance in certain regions, the decline in accuracy around the central area results in overall performance comparable to the original DINOv2 model. Finally, Fig. 6(c) shows that the model with both Lin and Lout successfully integrates the advantages of both loss functions. Furthermore, the accuracy drop observed in the central region in the models (a) and (b) is substantially mitigated in the model (c), resulting in an improvement in Acc. 4.7 Unsupervised object discovery The ability to focus on wide range of areas within images is also considered effective for object discovery. Therefore, we evaluate the unsupervised object discovery performance of our trained models. For the evaluation, we use LOST (Siméoni et al., 2021), which infers bounding boxes for objects from the patch tokens of features in the attention layers. Following Darcet et al. (2024) and Jiang et al. (2025), we present the best results of Correct Localization (CorLoc) across the key, query, or value features over the last four attention layers, and details of the evaluation setup are described in Sec. C.2. We utilize three datasets, VOC07 trainval, VOC12 trainval (Everingham et al., 2010), and COCO 20k (Lin et al., 2014; Vo et al., 2020). Table 2 presents the performance of four trained models on the unsupervised object discovery task. We observe that using Lin or Lout alone results in lower performance than the original DINOv2 model, except in the case of Lin on COCO. However, combining Lin and Lout outperforms the original model in all the three datasets. This improvement through combination is consistent with the results in the zero-shot image segmentation task. 8 Table 4: Focus-Oriented Image Retrieval performance. Classification performance. We evaluate our models on the ImageNet-1k classification task with k-NN (k = 20) and linear probing. Table 3 presents the top-1 accuracy on the validation set of ImageNet-1k. For k-NN classification, we observe that the accuracy drops by approximately 1 3% when visual focusing loss functions are introduced compared to the original DINOv2 model. Our possible explanation for the performance drop is as follows. The classification task is formulated as single-label problem, where images typically contain dominant object near the center. This task setting aligns with local-to-global correspondence for single objects in DINO (Caron et al., 2021). In contrast, our proposed loss functions are designed to capture wide range of regions and focus on various locations, and may therefore be less specialized for this setting. For linear probing classification, the accuracy difference between our visual focusing models and the original DINOv2 model is smaller than that observed with k-NN classification. This result suggests that training linear classifier for classification purposes enables effective utilization of the frozen features that have been pretrained to focus. Image retrieval performance. We also evaluate our models using an image retrieval task called focus-oriented image retrieval (FOIR) (Nozawa et al., 2025). FOIR task is multi-object image retrieval task that evaluates whether models can retrieve appropriate images for each specified object in query images, where the query images may contain multiple objects. We utilize COCO (Lin et al., 2014) and PASCAL VOC (Everingham et al., 2010) datasets for evaluation. We use Mean Precision at (MP@k) as an evaluation metric to measure the relevance of the top-k retrieved results. Table 4 presents MP@100 for each model and dataset. We evaluate models using two retrieval schemes. The first scheme, referred to as Fixed per image, utilizes single retrieval result obtained by extracting one feature vector from each query image for image retrieval. The second scheme, Visual prompt per object, applies PHS during inference and specifies bounding box for each object as visual prompt, thereby obtaining retrieval results that focus on individual objects. First, the consistent performance gain of the visual prompt per object scheme over the fixed per image one across the models indicates that PHS is effective during inference. In comparison between the models, under the fixed per image scheme, the original DINOv2 model outperforms the model with Lin and Lout; however, under the visual prompt per object scheme, the trend reverses, with the model with Lin and Lout outperforming the original DINOv2 model. This result suggests that the feature representations of DINOv2 effectively capture global image characteristics, resulting in averaged retrieval performance over objects, while the model with Lin and Lout, consistent with its training objective, exhibits its strengths when focusing on individual objects. 4.9 Additional results on model size variations To evaluate the robustness of our method, we further examine its effectiveness across different model sizes. Table 5 presents the zero-shot image segmentation performance of the original DINOv2 model and the model with Lin and Lout for ViT-B/16-Reg and ViT-g/16-Reg, evaluated in the same manner as for ViT-L/16-Reg. sections.title: 5 Discussion
sections.content: Local-to-global and region-to-focus correspondence. Our results highlight distinction between conventional local-to-global correspondence (Caron et al., 2021) and region-to-focus correspondence introduced by our visual focusing losses. The main DINOv2 objective is based on local-to-global correspondence and is well suited to images containing large dominant object, as it encourages correspondence between the global representation of the object and local representations of its In contrast, our method is designed for images containing multiple objects or semantic parts. regions, common setting in natural images. To address this setting, in addition to establishing local-to-global correspondence, our proposed loss functions encourage correspondence between regional representations obtained through masking or cropping and selective attention toward the corresponding regions. As observed in our experiments, this encourages the emergence of spatial attention head specialization, with performance gains in zero-shot image segmentation, unsupervised object discovery, and multi-object image retrieval. Practical implications. These properties may also have practical implications for interpretability and customizability. Distinct and spatially specialized attention heads can provide more structured view of the visual information captured by the model, potentially facilitating the analysis of its behavior and failure cases. Moreover, such specialization may offer straightforward mechanism for feature manipulation during inference. For example, the output features could be modified by dynamically disabling the signals from individual attention heads during inference, thereby potentially providing mechanism for on-the-fly model customization. These possibilities could be useful in applications that require selective or dynamically varying visual focus, such as robotic vision and autonomous driving. However, we do not evaluate such applications in this work, and their effectiveness remains an important direction for future investigation.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: Our work addresses key limitation of self-supervised ViT models by introducing visual focusing loss functions that establish correspondence between the models attention and specific regions within images. We find that diverse and spatially focused perceptual capabilities emerge in our trained model, enabling the model to leverage different attention heads to focus on distinct and meaningful image regions. This targeted focusing mechanism effectively mitigates the ambiguity and redundancy often observed in learned representations, thereby improving the interpretability of the models attention. Through comprehensive experiments, we demonstrate that our approach improves performance in zero-shot image segmentation, unsupervised object discovery, and multi-object image retrieval, while also producing clearer and more informative attention maps that support better visual understanding. Overall, these results highlight the potential of introducing focusing mechanisms into self-supervised representation learning without requiring annotations, providing new direction for learning diverse and spatially focused visual information. sections.title: A Limitations
sections.content: While our method can train the model to focus on diverse regions within an image, it does not allow explicit control over where each attention head focuses, as the regions of focus are determined implicitly during training. As result, it is not possible to know in advance which regions each attention head will focus on until after training. Our method also increases the training time and introduces trade-off between classification performance and performance improvements in zero-shot segmentation, object discovery, and FOIR tasks. Exploring other effective ways to utilize the visual focusing image representations obtained by our method remains an important direction for future work.

sections.title: B Societal impacts
sections.content: In this study, we propose self-supervised training method, and our trained models demonstrate high-performance segmentation across wide range of areas within images. Our method can identify both salient and subtle objects in images, and it has potential applications such as medical imaging, autonomous driving, and defect detection. However, incorrect segmentation of subtle structures may lead to erroneous decisions, posing risks especially in scenarios where safety is critical. The ability to extract subtle visible information also has risk of misuse, such as applying the method to privacy-invasive surveillance. To mitigate these concerns, we emphasize clear communication of limitations and intended use.

sections.title: C Details of training and evaluation setups
sections.content: C.1 Training Most of the training hyperparameters are identical to those used in Oquab et al. (2024) for training ViT-L/16 on ImageNet-1k. Here, we describe the differences from that setting. Due to computational resource constraints, we train the models using 4 NVIDIA H200 GPUs (141GB of memory), instead of 32 NVIDIA A100 GPUs (80GB of memory). Correspondingly, the batch size per GPU is set to 128 for the base and large models, and 64 for the giant models. In addition, for the models with registers, the number of registers is set to 4. Data augmentation. For each training image, following DINOv2, we apply multi-crop data augmentation, where global and local crops are generated using random resized cropping, together with standard augmentations such as horizontal flipping, color jittering, Gaussian blur, and solarization. The global crops are resized to 224 224 with scale = (0.32, 1.0) and ratio = (3.0/4.0, 4.0/3.0), while the local crops are resized to 96 96 with scale = (0.05, 0.32) and the same aspect-ratio range. When our loss functions Lin or Lout are introduced, box bx for the PHS method is obtained as region sampled via random resized cropping from the image, using the same setting as the local crops. We set the number of selected heads hon during training to 5 in our main experiments as discussed in Sec. D.4. For Lout, we also introduce randomness by selecting either the top or bottom edge of the visual-prompt box with equal probability for each batch and aligning the selected edge at the same height across all images in the batch. Training from scratch. The number of training iterations is set to 500,000. We set the base learning rate, which is the learning rate for batch size of 1024, to 0.004 for the base and large models, and 0.002 for the giant models for stable training. The training time for ViT-L/16-Reg is approximately 2 days and 22 hours for the DINOv2 model, 3 days and 21 hours for the model with Lin, 4 days and 11 hours for the model with Lout, and 5 days and 10 hours for the model with Lin and Lout. Pretrained models and continual learning. For our experiments about pretrained models in Sec. 4.1 and Sec. D.1, we compare DeiT III (Touvron et al., 2022), CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024) and DINOv2 with registers (Darcet et al., 2024), utilizing publicly available pretrained models. For DeiT III, we use the ViT-L/16 pretrained on ImageNet-1k at resolution of 224 224. For CLIP, we use the OpenCLIP implementation (Cherti et al., 2023) and employ the ViT-L/14 image encoder pretrained by OpenAI (Radford et al., 2021). For DINOv2 and DINOv2 with registers, we use the ViT-L/14 and the ViT-L/14-Reg, respectively, both pretrained on the large-scale LVD-142M dataset. We discuss continual learning using pretrained models in Sec. D.2. To match the patch size of 14, we change the local crops size from 96 to 98. During the initial training stage of the DINO head only, the number of iterations is set to 50,000. In the subsequent stage, where the entire networks are trained, we also set the number of iterations to 50,000. Throughout training, the base learning rate is set to 0.0004, and the number of warmup epochs is set to 1. The training dataset is the train split of ImageNet-1k dataset (Russakovsky et al., 2015) as in training from scratch. The training time for the DINO head of ViT-L/14-Reg is approximately 11 hours, and the training time for the entire networks is approximately 9 hours for the DINOv2 model, 12 hours for the model with Lin, 13 hours for the model with Lout, 16 hours for the model with Lin and Lout. C.2 Evaluation In all our evaluation experiments except unsupervised object discovery, the input images are resized to 224 224, whereas the unsupervised object discovery task does not involve resizing. For the unsupervised object discovery task, we utilize three datasets, VOC07 trainval (5,011 images), VOC12 trainval (11,540 images) (Everingham et al., 2010), and COCO 20k (19,817 images) (Lin et al., 2014; Vo et al., 2020). Following Darcet et al. (2024) and Jiang et al. (2025), we present the best results of CorLoc across the key, query, or value features over the last four attention layers, sweeping over manual bias term to the Gram matrix of features. We normalize the features and sweep the bias term over the range [1, 0] with step size of 0.01. The evaluation procedure for k-NN and linear probing classification follows that of Oquab et al. (2024). For linear probing classification, we report the highest accuracy performing the following grid search of three parameters: learning rate in {0.0001, 0.0002, 0.0005, 0.001, 0.002, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5}, number of output layers in {1, 4}, and concatenate average-pooled tokens in {yes, no}. The linear classifier is trained with SGD for 12,500 iterations. For the FOIR task, the evaluation procedure follows that of Nozawa et al. (2025). When the retrieval scheme is Visual prompt per object, the number of selected heads at evaluation is set to 2. We use two datasets for this evaluation: COCO (Lin et al., 2014) and PASCAL VOC (Everingham et al., 2010). COCO dataset contains 80 object categories, and we use val2017 for query images (5,000 images) and train2017 for database images (118,287 images). PASCAL VOC dataset contains 20 object categories, and we use test2007 for query images (4,952 images) and trainval2007+2012 for database images (16,551 images).

sections.title: D Extended analyses
sections.content: D.1 Extended results on interpretability of attention maps for conventional training methods In addition to our experiment in Sec. 4.1, we conduct extended analyses on the interpretability of attention maps obtained using four different training methods: DeiT III (Touvron et al., 2022), CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024) and DINOv2 with registers (Darcet et al., 2024), utilizing publicly available pretrained models. Table A1 presents comparison of zero-shot image segmentation performance of each training method. This result shows that DINOv2 and DINOv2 with registers outperform the other methods. As shown in Fig. A1, the impact of these artifacts is substantial for DeiT III and CLIP, leading to low interpretability of the attention maps. In contrast, DINOv2 produces single patch that appears to be an artifact, while the remaining patches capture meaningful image information, resulting in meaningful mask. In DINOv2 with registers, the register tokens are effective in suppressing artifacts, and the object regions are captured more clearly. D.2 Continual learning in existing models In this subsection, we consider applying our training method to continual learning in existing models. For the pretrained model, we utilize the publicly available backbone ViT-L/14-Reg weights pretrained by DINOv2 with registers (Darcet et al., 2024), which we evaluate in Sec. 4.1 and Sec. D.1. Since pretrained weights of the DINO head is not available, we first train the DINO head using DINOv2 with registers from scratch, while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen. After training the DINO head, we then perform training the entire networks, using each loss function with fewer iterations Table A1: Zero-shot image segmentation performance comparison of four training methods (a)-(d). Table A2 presents comparison of zero-shot image segmentation performance between the pretrained model and models further trained using four different loss functions. On ImageNet-Segmentation dataset, the performance improves with all loss functions used for continual learning, with the DINOv2 model with Lin and Lout achieving the highest performance. On PASCAL VOC dataset, the DINOv2 loss, DINOv2 loss with Lin, and DINOv2 loss with Lout all show performance degradation across all metrics. The discrepancy between the results on ImageNet-Segmentation and PASCAL VOC can be attributed to the domain gap between these datasets. While further training on ImageNet1k improves performance on the in-domain dataset ImageNet-Segmentation, it results in degradation in the out-of-domain dataset PASCAL VOC. Notably, the DINOv2 loss with both Lin and Lout improves performance on two out of three metrics, mIoU and mAP. This indicates that combination of Lin and Lout exhibits stronger robustness to domain shifts and better generalization ability. D.3 Loss weights analysis We investigate the effects of loss weights (win, wout) in Eq. (4) that balance the DINO loss LDINO and the two visual focusing loss functions Lin and Lout on segmentation performance. In this experiment, we train ViT-L/16 with Lin, one with Lout, and one with Lin and Lout with weights set to 0.05 and 0.1, respectively. The results in Tab. A4 show that introducing each weight of 0.05 leads to substantial improvement in performance compared to the original DINOv2 model, whereas increasing the weights to 0.1 slightly degrades performance compared to 0.05. These findings indicate that simply increasing the weights of Lin and Lout is not necessarily beneficial; rather, balancing between the visual focusing loss and the DINO loss is crucial for achieving optimal performance. We conduct these analyses on training the ViT model without registers and find that the resulting loss weights also perform well with the ViT model incorporating registers. Therefore, we apply these weights in the experiments presented in the main results of our paper. D.4 Analysis of the number of selected heads during training The number of selected heads hon during training is hyperparameter of our training method. The number hon refers to the number of heads selected during head selection in PHS, and it affects training through changes in the output of the student model PHS . To investigate the effect of hon on performance, we train ViT-L/16 by varying hon across three settings: {2, 5, 8}. Tables A5 and A6 show the effect of hon on the performance for the zero-shot image segmentation task and the FOIR task, respectively. For hon = 2, the models achieve high performance on the segmentation task, whereas their performance on the FOIR task is relatively low. In the case of hon = 8, while the model with Lin and Lout exhibits high performance on the FOIR task, the performance is relatively low for other models and tasks. Since hon = 5 yields consistently high performance overall, we adopt hon = 5. We find that the resulting value hon = 5 also performs well with the ViT model incorporating registers. It is confirmed that the properties of attention maps discussed in Sec. 4.5 are consistent across different examples. D.6 Entropy analysis of attention To complement our qualitative visualizations of attention maps in Fig. 4, we additionally conduct quantitative analysis of spatial attention head specialization. Specifically, we compute the Shannon entropy of the attention distribution underlying the attention maps. Table A7 shows the following two metrics: (1) Mean Per-Head Entropy: the entropy is first computed separately for each head and then averaged across heads, and (2) Entropy of Head-Averaged Attention: the attention distributions are first averaged across heads, after which the entropy is computed. These entropies are normalized, such that uniform attention distribution has the maximum value of 1. We use models evaluated in Fig. 4 and report averages over the validation set of ImageNet-1k. Our Lin & Lout model exhibits lower mean per-head entropy than the original DINOv2 model but high entropy after averaging attention across heads, indicating that individual heads produce spatially concentrated attention, while their aggregation covers broad range of image regions. This result provides quantitative evidence of spatial specialization and diversity across attention heads. (2026). We conduct the evaluations on ADE20k (Zhou et al., 2017), Cityscapes (Cordts et al., 2016), and PASCAL VOC 2012 (VOC) (Everingham et al., 2015). For VOC, we train the models on the trainaug dataset (Hariharan et al., 2011). We perform hyperparameter sweep varying the learning rate over {1 104, 3 104, 1 103} and weight decay over {1 104, 1 103}. Table A8 compares the supervised semantic segmentation performance of our Lin & Lout model with that of the original DINOv2 model. In terms of model scaling, for both DINOv2 and our model, the Large variant outperforms the Base variant in supervised semantic segmentation. However, in the zero-shot segmentation setting of Tabs. 1 and 5, we observe the opposite trend, with the Base variant outperforming the Large variant. This trend is consistent with both previous work (Stegmüller et al., 2025) and our additional evaluation of the publicly available pretrained DINOv2 models under the same zero-shot segmentation protocol (Tab. A9). Regarding method comparison in Tab. A8, our Lin & Lout model consistently outperforms the original DINOv2 model across all three datasets for the Base model size. For the Large model size, the Lin & Lout model demonstrates superior performance on Cityscapes, while the original DINOv2 model achieves better results on ADE20k and VOC. Nevertheless, the performance differences between the two models are small in the supervised semantic segmentation setting, with both achieving competitive results and exhibiting no clear performance advantage over one another. These findings clarify that the distinctive property of our model, namely spatial attention head specialization, enables the direct extraction of high-quality features from attention maps in zero-shot setting while maintaining competitive performance on the supervised downstream task of semantic segmentation.
